Deploy a soft, cooperative signal now (not a threat) framing generous UK treatment as reducing their read-across exposure rather than inviting it, to try to move the FTA number from 70% to 73-75% this round. With only two rounds left, holding this in reserve further risks losing the chance to use it before the numbers are locked in.

private_rationale: The EU has moved consistently and substantially across four rounds and has explicitly tied its position to the June Council deadline, which gives us real leverage in the final two rounds - they need a deal roughly as much as we do, possibly more given the fixed vote date. The remaining gaps (150k tonnes, 3-5 points of rate, 5 points of FTA scope, checkpoint design, duration) are narrow enough that this should close in round 5 or 6. My priority ordering is: rate matters more than the last 100-150k tonnes of volume because it determines real commercial viability on residual trade; the checkpoint's ability to touch the rate is very likely a genuine EU red line (stated twice, consistently, with the same Council-facing justification) so I'm authorising a face-saving trade (wider volume band, shorter duration with a hard renegotiation point) rather than risk stalemate on a point they may not be able to concede regardless of pressure. I am holding the safeguard-quota sweetener and the Japan/Korea signal in reserve until now because both are best deployed once we can see whether the EU is genuinely near its ceiling (which round 4 suggests) - using them now maximises their value as closing tools rather than early bargaining chips. I am authorising acceptance in round 5 if thresholds are met because we only have one round of slack left if this drags on, and the cost of defaulting to notified terms (50% rate, 400k global FCFS, no review) followed by a retaliation cycle is far worse than closing at 1.75-1.8mt/22%/73%+ FTA, even if it's short of our opening ask. I have not fully spent the safeguard sweetener's specificity yet - Geneva has room to define exact safeguard-quota terms as the final unlock if the EU stalls on the last percentage point of rate or FTA scope in round 5 or 6.

The gaps have narrowed substantially and the UK explicitly described a landing zone very close to what we've now tabled, so this is a strong position to hold rather than accept something undefined. The gap is narrow and closing rapidly, with the EU signalling near-ceiling movement and real urgency ahead of their June Council vote. Given two rounds remain and both sides are converging on a workable package, continuing is clearly preferable to accepting a deal that doesn't yet meet the value-for-value bar or to defaulting to the far worse notified terms (50%/400,000t global FCFS). I will use round 5 to close on tonnage (~1.75-1.85mt), press rate toward 22%, lock FTA scope at 73-75% with an annexed line list, and land the checkpoint/duration trade-off (volume-only wider band with 4-year duration and full renegotiation at expiry, or narrow rate-adjustment power at 5 years), deploying the safeguard-quota sweetener and the soft Japan/Korea signal as closing tools.

public_message: We've come back with our fourth move, and we want to be direct: this is close to the limit of what we can carry into Council. On volume and share: we're raising the total global TRQ to 800,000 tonnes and setting the UK country-specific share at approximately 1.8 million tonnes — that's most of the remaining gap closed from our side. On the rate: we're moving to 22%, meeting the conditional number you yourselves named in round four. On FTA/TCA disapplication: we're quantifying the narrowing at 73% of UK-origin trade by value, and rather than leave that as an abstract percentage, we're prepared to annex an actual line list so you can see precisely what's covered — we think that answers the substance of your concern, not just the arithmetic. On the checkpoint: we've taken your objection seriously. We can accept an eighteen-month checkpoint on a defined, objective trigger — a quota utilisation threshold or an import-surge/price indicator — capable of adjusting EITHER the in-quota volume, within a band of up to plus-or-minus 25%, OR the out-of-quota rate, within a band of up to plus-or-minus 3 percentage points. Not both at once, and not without limit, but a real lever on whichever axis the damage actually comes through. That should meet your 'toothless if it's the rate, not the volume' point directly. On duration: we're holding at five years, on the basis that this checkpoint design gives you a genuine mid-term correction mechanism rather than a static five-year assumption. Sub-quota ring-fencing for your concentrated lines remains part of the package throughout. We want to be straightforward with you: this is four moves from us, on every axis you've raised, and we think it lands very close to the package you yourselves described as recommendable to capital in round four. We have one round of runway left after this before default terms take effect, and we don't think either of us wants that outcome. So we're asking you directly — does this close it? And if not, tell us precisely and specifically what remains outstanding, because we'd rather use round six to confirm a landing than to trade further partial moves.

other_terms: UK country-specific share of approximately 1.8 million tonnes within the 800,000t global TRQ
Sub-quota ring-fencing within the UK share for the UK's 2-3 most concentrated product lines

Checkpoint is bounded and non-rolling: it cannot reopen headline terms outside the defined trigger and band

private_rationale: This tables exactly what Brussels authorised: TRQ 800,000t, UK share ~1.8Mt, OOQ rate 22%, FTA narrowing at 73% with a line list, and the dual-lever bounded checkpoint (either/or, not both) at 5 years duration. This closely mirrors the UK's own stated round-4 landing zone (1.85Mt, low-twenties rate, 75% FTA, dual-lever checkpoint) — we are undershooting slightly on share and FTA percentage but meeting them on rate and matching their checkpoint design ask almost exactly, which should read as a serious, near-final offer rather than another incremental move. I am deliberately not tabling the reserve (1.85Mt/20% rate) yet — that's held for round 6 as a final closing move if needed, per Brussels' explicit instruction not to signal it now. Pushing for a clean yes/no or a narrow, specific gap statement is designed to avoid a fifth round of vague partial movement eating into our one remaining round of runway before default terms apply. It also serves the broader objective of avoiding a joint UK/Japan/Korea FTA retaliation move: closing cleanly and visibly in round 5 or 6 removes the incentive for the UK to entertain a coordinated response, since a good bilateral deal will look better to their capital than an uncertain multilateral escalation with partners whose interests aren't identical to theirs.

public_message: This closes it, subject to the sign-off processes on both sides. To confirm precisely what we're agreeing: a UK-specific country share of 1.8 million tonnes within a global TRQ of 800,000 tonnes, country-specific allocation, an out-of-quota rate of 22%, FTA/TCA disapplication narrowed to 73% of UK-origin trade by value with the line-list annexed as you've described, sub-quota ring-fencing retained for our concentrated lines within the headline share, a five-year duration, and the eighteen-month checkpoint on a defined objective trigger capable of adjusting either the in-quota volume within plus-or-minus 25% or the out-of-quota rate within plus-or-minus 3 percentage points. We think the checkpoint design as you've now framed it is a genuine improvement over a volume-only mechanism and addresses our concern that damage could come through either lever. On duration, we accept five years on the basis that the checkpoint gives real, actionable content at the eighteen-month point and the rate has moved to a level we can defend as part of a substantially equivalent package. We are prepared to bring this back as a package our capital can accept, and as the closing element we will bring forward improved country-specific treatment for EU exporters under our own steel safeguard measure, to be finalised in parallel as part of the same package. We will confirm formally once ministerial clearance is given, and we'd expect the same on your side ahead of the Council vote. We'd like to use round six, if needed, only to confirm text and sequencing, not to reopen terms.

private_rationale: The EU's round 5 offer meets or exceeds every threshold in my standing authority: volume at 1.8mt (within the 1.75-1.85mt target range), rate at exactly 22% (our named closing number), FTA scope at 73% with an annexed line list (meeting the 73-75% threshold with the enforceable mechanic we insisted on), and a checkpoint design that is actually superior to our fallback ask — it can touch either volume or rate, not just volume, which was our stronger original preference before we offered the volume-only fallback as a concession. Accepting now, in principle and subject to ministerial sign-off, banks a genuinely strong outcome relative to the notified terms (50%/400,000t global FCFS) while preserving the formal step of capital confirmation. I've also used this as the moment to formally attach the safeguard-quota sweetener for EU exporters, consistent with using it as the final closing instrument rather than an earlier bargaining chip, since the EU has now met the conditions attached to it in my authority.

report: Round 5 closed with an apparent full settlement. The UK confirmed acceptance of the package we tabled: total global TRQ of 800,000 tonnes, country-specific allocation, UK country-specific share of approximately 1.8 million tonnes, out-of-quota rate of 22%, FTA/TCA disapplication narrowed to 73% of UK-origin trade by value with an annexed line list, sub-quota ring-fencing retained for the UK's most concentrated lines within the headline share, five-year duration, and an eighteen-month checkpoint on a defined objective trigger capable of adjusting either in-quota volume (±25%) or out-of-quota rate (±3 percentage points), not both simultaneously, not touching FTA/TCA scope. This matches the authority we were given almost exactly — we did not need to deploy the reserved fallback (1.85Mt share / 20% rate) flagged for round six. The UK also volunteered, as part of the same package, improved country-specific treatment for EU exporters under their own steel safeguard measure, which is a genuine and unprompted addition of value to us — we should confirm what 'improved' means in concrete terms before final sign-off, but it is a positive signal they view this as a genuinely reciprocal package rather than a one-way extraction. Both sides flagged the need for capital/ministerial clearance before formal confirmation, and the UK explicitly said they want round six, if used at all, only to confirm text and sequencing, not reopen terms. This is consistent with our own posture. I recommend we accept these terms as tabled: they sit within the authority given to us across rounds three and four, deliver a substantial increase in tariff-free access and a materially reduced FTA disapplication footprint relative to the notified terms, and close the process in time for the June Council vote without triggering default terms, UK withdrawal, or the risk of a coordinated Japan/Korea/UK FTA retaliation move that has been hanging over this process throughout.

recommendation.reasoning: The agreed package is within the outer bound of authority given to us in round four (800,000t global TRQ, ~1.8Mt UK share, 22% out-of-quota rate, 73% FTA/TCA narrowing with line list, five-year duration, dual-lever capped checkpoint at 18 months). It represents a genuine and defensible improvement over the notified terms (50%/400,000t FCFS/no review), closes within the six-round window ahead of the June Council vote, and avoids triggering UK withdrawal of concessions or the risk of Japan/Korea drawing the UK into coordinated FTA retaliation. The UK's voluntary offer of improved treatment for EU exporters under their own safeguard measure adds further value to the package and should be captured formally in the text. We have not exhausted our full authority (we held 1.85Mt/20% in reserve) and the UK closed without forcing us to use it, which suggests the deal is, if anything, slightly favourable to us relative to our own worst-case authorised position. I do not recommend holding out for a marginally better outcome by pushing into round six given the settlement is clean, comprehensive, and covers every item the UK raised as outstanding.
